title: Nehemiah 1:1–3
context: Nehemiah 1:1–3 opens the memoir of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, written largely in the first person. In the month Chislev of the twentieth year, while Nehemiah is in Susa the palace, Hanani and some men from Judah report that the survivors of the captivity in the province are in great affliction and reproach, and that Jerusalem’s wall is broken down and its gates burned. Verse 1 does not name the king, but 2:1 dates the next scene to the twentieth year of Artaxerxes, and Nehemiah later speaks of serving as governor “from the twentieth year even to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes the king” (5:14). Chislev in 1:1 and Nisan in 2:1 are both placed in the twentieth year, although Nisan usually comes earlier in the year; interpreters explain this in different ways, for example by a different way of counting the regnal year, and this draft does not decide. Hanani is called “one of my brothers”, which may mean a brother or more broadly a kinsman; 7:2 later names “my brother Hanani” as one placed in charge of Jerusalem. It is also uncertain whether the damage reported is the Babylonian destruction of the walls (2 Kings 25:10) or more recent harm, perhaps connected with the halted building in Ezra 4:7–23. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground: Nehemiah’s grief begins with honest attention to the condition of God’s people.

verses.text: The words of Nehemiah the son of Hacaliah. Now in the month Chislev, in the twentieth year, as I was in Susa the palace,
verses.arminianNotes:
The book opens with the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, who is in Susa the palace in the month Chislev of the twentieth year. The king is not named here; 2:1 supplies Artaxerxes, and how the months fit the regnal year is discussed.

Arminian readers note that the memoir begins with a real person in a real place, and they see God’s purposes for Jerusalem advancing through an ordinary servant’s willing response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the story begins far from Jerusalem, in the Persian court, and they see God’s providence placing his servant where he will be needed long before Nehemiah knows his part.

Both traditions read the opening as shared ground and hold the dating questions with appropriate caution.

verses.text: Hanani, one of my brothers, came, he and certain men out of Judah; and I asked them about the Jews who had escaped, who were left of the captivity, and concerning Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Hanani, one of Nehemiah’s brothers, comes with men from Judah, and Nehemiah asks about the Jews who had escaped and survived the captivity, and about Jerusalem. The word brothers may mean a brother or a kinsman; 7:2 names “my brother Hanani”.

Arminian readers note that Nehemiah takes the initiative to ask, showing a genuine concern for his people that God will use.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Nehemiah’s concern for a distant city reflects a heart bound to God’s people and his promises, and they see in his question the beginning of a work God is preparing.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground: caring enough to ask about the condition of God’s people is the first step toward serving them.

verses.text: They said to me, “The remnant who are left of the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach. The wall of Jerusalem is also broken down, and its gates are burned with fire.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They report that the remnant left of the captivity in the province are in great affliction and reproach, and that Jerusalem’s wall is broken down and its gates burned with fire. Whether this is the old Babylonian destruction or more recent damage is uncertain.

Arminian readers see an honest report that calls for a response, and they note that the people’s reproach is a real need that faithful people are summoned to meet.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the reproach of God’s people touches the honor of God’s name, since Jerusalem was the city where he had chosen to place his name, and they see the report as preparing for a prayer grounded in that concern.

Both traditions read the verse as shared ground and treat the distress of God’s people with seriousness.
